notes: Story beat per the brief: the morning walk, Alke and the hare, the stele, the tithe, "not today".

Segments s052–s055 are Xenophon, Anabasis 5.3.13 (the inscription, as printed in design §3.2), shown receptively and glossed; its ἂν … ποιῇ is outside the Unit 1 licence. Xenophon paraphrases it at once in licensed Greek.
Edition conventions: capital only at a paragraph start and at the start of direct speech; «» for speech; movable ν before a vowel and at a pause.
Reasons for the temple (design §3.2, Anab. 5.3.4–9): a tithe of the spoils for Artemis, no vow.

cover.alt: Early morning at Scillus. A bearded man in his forties walks down a grassy slope from a farmhouse towards a small river with two boys; an old man follows holding three hounds on leads. Across the river a wooded hill rises, and at the edge of the wood stands a small temple with a stone stele beside it. Horses graze in a meadow in front of the house.
cover.art_brief: Spring, about 384 BC, just after sunrise: low gold light from the left, dew, fresh green. Estate of Xenophon at Scillus in Triphylia (Anab. 5.3.7-13). Left: a modest Greek farmhouse (whitewashed mudbrick on stone footing, tiled roof, a walled yard) on a gentle slope; in front of it a meadow with three or four horses grazing. Centre: a path down to a small clear river (the Selinus), shallow, with stones, a few reeds. Right, beyond the river: a hill covered with oak and wild pear wood; at the near edge of the wood a SMALL Ionic temple (a miniature of Ephesus: four columns, pale stone), and beside it a plain upright stone stele about head-high with lettering (lettering illegible, NOT readable Greek). Figures on the path, walking towards the river: Xenophon (about 45, short dark beard going grey, plain undyed wool chiton and a light cloak, walking staff, bareheaded); Gryllus (12, dark hair, eager, a step ahead, short chiton); Diodorus (10, smaller, curly hair, looking towards the temple); behind them Sosias (about 60, Thracian, weathered, grey beard, patterned Thracian cap, holding three lean Laconian hounds on leather leads: one tawny female (Alke), one black female (Psyche), one brindled male (Thymos)). Realistic watercolour-and-ink style; no text, no modern objects.

inference_aids.alt: In the foreground a tawny hound with a trailing lead leaps through a shallow river after a hare. On the far bank nobody has noticed: a bearded man with a staff points away, two boys look where he points, and an old man in a fox-skin cap bends over two hounds; a farmhouse and horses are behind them.
inference_aids.art_brief: Same morning, a few minutes later. Shallow river (the Selinus) with stones, splashes. Mid-picture: a brown hare in full stride leaping out of the water on the far bank, heading up a slope towards an oak wood; just behind it in mid-river the tawny hound Alke, ears back, running. A trailing leather lead flies loose behind Alke. Near bank, foreground: NOBODY has noticed (the text says οὐδὲ οἱ παῖδες ᾔσθοντο). Xenophon (45, staff) points away to the left, towards distant Olympia; Gryllus (12) and Diodorus (10) look where he points, their backs half turned to the river; Sosias (old Thracian, grey beard, patterned cap) bends over the two other hounds (black Psyche, brindled Thymos) on leads, untangling them. Far up the hill at the edge of the wood, small and distant, the little temple. Watercolour-and-ink, same character designs as the cover; no text.

inference_aids.alt: Beside a small temple at the edge of a wood, a tawny hound lies panting at the foot of an inscribed stone stele. A small boy stands at the stele tracing the letters with his finger; an older boy crouches by the dog; an old man with two hounds and a bearded man approach.
inference_aids.art_brief: Later the same morning, light through oak leaves. A small Ionic temple of pale stone (four columns, a miniature of the Artemision at Ephesus) at the edge of a wood, with a few cultivated fruit trees around it (Anab. 5.3.12). In front of it an upright stone stele, about as tall as a man, inscribed with several lines of Greek capitals (letters may be suggested, but must NOT form real or fake readable words). At the foot of the stele: Alke, the tawny hound, lying on her side, tongue out, exhausted, no hare anywhere. Diodorus (10) stands close to the stele, one finger on the lettering, mouth moving (reading aloud slowly). Gryllus (12) crouches by Alke, scolding her with a raised finger. Behind, coming out of the trees: Sosias with the two other hounds on leads, and Xenophon (45, staff), smiling a little. Watercolour-and-ink, same character designs; no legible text.

grammar.title: Ποῦ; ποῖ; πόθεν;
grammar.rule: ποῦ; ἐν + dat. · ποῖ; εἰς / πρός + acc. · πόθεν; ἐκ / ἀπό + gen. · ἀνα-βαίνω → ἀν-έ-βη
grammar.note_en:
Where, whither, whence. Greek asks three questions about place: ποῦ; (where is it?), ποῖ; (where is it going?) and πόθεν; (where is it coming from?). Each has its usual answers: ἐν + dative for position; εἰς "into, to" or πρός "towards, up to" + accusative for destination; ἐκ "out of" or ἀπό "away from" + genitive for source. Strictly it is the preposition and its meaning that choose the case, so learn these as pairs rather than as a rule that ποῦ; always wants a dative. Sosias answers ποῖ; and ποῦ; in one breath: εἰς τὴν ὕλην εἰσῆλθεν … καὶ νῦν ἐν τῇ ὕλῃ ἐστίν (s031). To Diodorus's πόθεν; he says ἀπὸ τοῦ ποταμοῦ (s041).

παρά shows the pattern most clearly, because it takes all three cases: the dative usually marks being beside someone or something, the accusative going up to it, the genitive coming away from it. (παρά + accusative can also mean simply "alongside", as on the stele by the temple in the Anabasis.) Xenophon stood παρὰ τῷ ποταμῷ, beside the river (s008); Gryllus went παρὰ τὴν Ἀλκήν, up to Alke (s048); and he slipped away παρὰ τοῦ πατρός, from his father (s073). With persons, παρά is the ordinary word for "at the house of, to, from"; with places Greek prefers ἐν, εἰς, πρός, ἐκ and ἀπό. ὑπέρ + genitive "above" and πρό + genitive "in front of" describe the estate in s010 and s009.

Preverbs of motion. The same prepositions are fixed to verbs of motion as preverbs: ἀνα- up, κατα- down, δια- across or through, εἰσ- in, ἐκ- out, ἀπο- away, προσ- towards. A compound often repeats its preposition in the phrase: εἰς τὴν ὕλην εἰσῆλθε, ἐκ τῆς ὕλης ἐξῆλθον, πρὸς τὸν ναὸν προσῆλθον (s045). διαβαίνω takes a plain accusative of the thing crossed: διέβη τὸν ποταμόν (s027).

The augment goes inside. The augment belongs to the simple verb, so in a past indicative it stands between the preverb and the stem: ἀνα + ἔβη → ἀνέβη, κατα + ἔβησαν → κατέβησαν, ἀπο + ἦλθε → ἀπῆλθε. A preverb that ends in a vowel drops it before the augment (ἀν-, κατ-, δι-, ἀπ-); περι- and προ- keep theirs, as later units will show. ἐκ becomes ἐξ before any vowel: ἐξῆλθε. εἰσ- and προσ- already end in a consonant: εἰσῆλθε, προσῆλθε. ἀναγιγνώσκω "read" works the same way in the imperfect: ἀνεγίγνωσκεν (s051).

Outside the indicative there is no augment, and the preverb keeps its own shape: ἀναβῆναι (s017), ἀπελθοῦσα (s024), καταβαίνετε (s071). So ἀπελθοῦσα, never *ἀπηλθοῦσα: the participle has no augment to lose.

To find the dictionary form of a compound, take the augment out and give the preverb back its vowel: διέβη → δια-βαίνω, κατέβησαν → κατα-βαίνω, ἐξῆλθον → ἐκ + ἔρχομαι = ἐξέρχομαι. The table is for looking things up, not for learning by heart.

parergon.title: μέν … δέ
parergon.body_en: μέν … δέ sets two things side by side. English rarely needs "on the one hand … on the other": usually "while", "but", or nothing at all. μέν comes after the first word or phrase of the first half and usually tells you a δέ is coming: ὁ μὲν λαγὼς ἔφευγεν, ἡ δὲ Ἀλκὴ ἐδίωκεν (s026). It sorts time (πρῶτον μὲν … ἔπειτα δέ, s027), people (Ἐγὼ μὲν … Ἐγὼ δέ, s016–s017) and things (ταῦτα μὲν … ταῦτα δέ, s039); the inscription uses it for the owner's two duties (τὴν μὲν δεκάτην … ἐκ δὲ τοῦ περιττοῦ). δέ alone, also placed after the first word, means "and" or "but" and moves the story on.

ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄρους πρὸς τὸν ποταμὸν βαίνω (↔ ἀναβαίνω)

families.spelling_note: A preverb is written as it sounds next to what follows. ἐκ becomes ἐξ before a vowel: ἐξ-ῆλθε, ἐξ-έρχομαι. ἀπο-, κατα-, ἀνα-, δια- drop their final vowel before a vowel: ἀπ-ῆλθε, κατ-έβη, ἀν-έβη, δι-έβη. Before a rough breathing the consonant is aspirated as well: ἀπ’ → ἀφ’ (ἀφ-ικνέομαι), κατ’ → καθ’ (καθ-ίστημι). The same happens to the free prepositions: ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ, ἀφ’ ἡμῶν, κατ’ αὐτόν, καθ’ ἡμέραν.

diagram.alt: A cross-section of the estate: a house on level ground on the left, a slope down to a river in the middle, and across it a hill rising to a small temple at the edge of an oak wood on the right. Labelled arrows: ἐκ- out through the house door, ἀπο- away from the house on its other side, κατα- down the slope to the river, δια- across the river, ἀνα- up the hill, προσ- towards the temple, εἰσ- into the wood.
